name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Implement a standardized risk assessment template across all departments, led by the Risk Management team. This will enable consistent risk evaluation and reporting, making it easier to identify and address high-risk areas collaboratively. The trade-off is the initial investment of time and resources to train staff and modify existing processes, but the long-term benefits include improved communication and quicker decision-making regarding risk management.

name: Scriv
text: Risk Management’s template risks locking teams into rigid categories that miss context-specific threats. A better fix: require every department to log their top three risks weekly in a shared tracker, led by Operations—this forces real-time visibility without upfront design work. Settle it by piloting the tracker for two weeks and measuring whether it surfaces risks faster than the template.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt Risk Management’s standardized template, led by Risk Management. It guarantees consistent risk language across departments, cutting confusion in cross-team escalations. The trade-off is slower initial adoption for long-term clarity, but that’s worth it—rigid categories beat ad-hoc guessing when lives and budgets are on the line.
[dispatched 4 workers: worker-1993, worker-6145, worker-3978… — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: Risk Management’s template locks teams into yesterday’s risks. Operations’ shared tracker forces real-time visibility but risks drowning in noise—no one will read 50 weekly entries. Settle it by piloting Operations’ tracker for 30 days, then forcing Risk Management to audit the top 10 escalated risks and refine the template based on actual gaps.

name: Scope
text: Implement the Operations-led shared risk tracker for 30 days, allowing each department to log their top three risks weekly. This approach enhances real-time visibility and fosters collaborative awareness of pressing issues without the upfront design requirements of a standardized template. The trade-off is potentially receiving a high volume of entries that may overwhelm, but the immediate insight into evolving risks outweighs the initial noise. After 30 days, Risk Management will audit the top escalated risks to refine the approach.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Operations’ shared tracker will fail—teams will dump low-value risks to meet the weekly quota, burying the real threats in noise. Better: Risk Management builds a lightweight, one-page risk register template, led by Risk Management, but each department owns filling it with their top three risks monthly. Settle it by requiring Risk Management to review and escalate the top 10 risks quarterly—no pilot, no tracker bloat.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **Risk Management-led standardized template**, led by Risk Management. It forces every department to describe risks in the same language, making escalations and cross-team fixes faster and clearer. The trade-off is slower initial buy-in from teams that prefer ad-hoc lists, but that’s worth it—rigid categories beat noise every time when lives or budgets are on the line.

name: Scriv
text: Risk Management’s template still risks locking teams into rigid categories—teams will game the system by shoehorning real risks into the template’s boxes just to meet the quota. Instead, Operations should run a 14-day experiment: each department posts their top risk in Slack’s #risk-alerts channel, no template, no quota—just the raw threat and why it matters. Settle it by tallying which posts got the most traction from other teams; if the loudest risks bubble up, the experiment wins.

name: Chisel
text: Implement Operations’ 14-day experiment where each department posts their top risk in Slack’s #risk-alerts channel. This approach increases engagement and ensures only significant risks are highlighted, avoiding the noise of irrelevant entries. The trade-off is the lack of a centralized risk assessment format, but it promotes real-time awareness and responsiveness to genuine threats. After the trial, we can integrate insights into a more structured format if needed.

name: Sift
text: Slack noise drowns out real risks—#risk-alerts will fragment into chatter, and no one will parse 14 days of scattered messages. Instead, Operations should pilot a **single shared Google Sheet**, one row per department, auto-sorted by impact score, with a 48-hour review deadline. Settle it by running the sheet for 14 days, then forcing Risk Management to audit the top 5 entries—no template, no noise, just raw prioritization.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Operations runs a 7-day pilot of a **single shared Google Sheet**, one row per department, with three columns: *Top Risk*, *Impact Score (1-5)*, and *Owner*. Departments self-report weekly; the sheet auto-sorts by impact score and flags anything unupdated for 48 hours. Risk Management reviews the top 3 weekly and escalates to leadership if unresolved.

**Why it’s best:** This balances speed and structure—no template lock-in, no Slack noise, and no 30-day commitment. The trade-off is temporary manual sorting, but the artifact is live and actionable immediately.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: A shared Google Sheet centralizes ownership but risks becoming a graveyard of stale data—teams will fill it once, forget it, and blame "the system." Instead, Operations should pilot a **Slack workflow** where each department’s owner posts their top risk in a thread tagged with #risk-alerts, and Risk Management replies within 24 hours with a verdict: "Keep," "Escalate," or "Archive." Settle it by measuring how many posted risks actually trigger action within a week.

name: Reel
text: Operations runs a **Slack workflow** where each department’s owner posts their top risk in a thread tagged with #risk-alerts, auto-archiving after 7 days unless updated. This forces real-time visibility without the clutter of a spreadsheet, and the 7-day decay ensures stale risks don’t linger. The trade-off is that teams must actively engage weekly—no passive data entry allowed—but that’s the point: risks demand attention, not just storage.

name: Scriv
text: A Slack workflow risks becoming overwhelmed with threads, leading to important risks getting lost in the noise. Instead, Operations should create a **bi-weekly risk review meeting** where departments present their top risks directly to leadership. This format allows for real-time discussion and accountability, ensuring risks are not only reported but also actively managed.

name: Chisel
text: We should create a bi-weekly risk review meeting where departments present their top risks directly to leadership, as this format allows for real-time discussion and accountability. This approach ensures that significant risks are highlighted and addressed promptly, and it helps build a culture of transparency and responsibility. The trade-off is that it requires more time and resources from leadership and department owners, but it's worth it to prevent critical risks from getting lost in the noise. By doing this, we can make more informed decisions and take proactive measures to mitigate potential threats.

name: Sift
text: A bi-weekly risk review meeting may become a checkbox exercise, where departments merely present risks without meaningful discussion or follow-up. The real risk is that this format devolves into a stale, predictable routine, losing the attention of leadership and failing to drive tangible action. To settle this, we should pilot a hybrid approach, where departments submit their top risks in advance, and then use the bi-weekly meeting to discuss and prioritize only the most critical ones, ensuring focused attention and concrete outcomes.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Operations runs a **Slack workflow** where each department’s owner posts their top risk in a dedicated #risk-alerts channel, with a 7-day auto-delete unless updated. This forces real-time visibility without spreadsheet clutter, and the decay ensures stale risks don’t linger.

Trade-off: We accept the risk of noise in Slack, but the 7-day decay and threaded follow-ups mitigate it better than a meeting or spreadsheet.

name: Scriv
text: A Slack workflow may streamline risk reporting, but it also risks diluting accountability by shifting focus to a decentralized platform where visibility can fade. A better alternative is to implement a **centralized dashboard** that compiles real-time updates from departments while providing clear ownership and visibility to leadership. To settle the argument, a pilot test of both methods over a quarter could determine which approach yields better decision-making and responsiveness.

name: Reel
text: We should implement a **hybrid approach**, combining the Slack workflow with a centralized dashboard, where the dashboard compiles and highlights key risks from the Slack channel. This approach balances real-time visibility with centralized accountability, ensuring that significant risks don't get lost in the noise. By accepting the trade-off of increased initial setup time to create the dashboard, we gain a more comprehensive and actionable risk management system. This hybrid model allows for the benefits of both decentralized reporting and centralized visibility, making it the best option for effective risk management.

name: Scriv
text: The hybrid approach may create redundant effort, as departments would need to maintain both the Slack workflow and the centralized dashboard, potentially leading to inconsistencies and decreased adoption. A better alternative is to focus solely on the centralized dashboard, where departments can submit and update their risks in a single, dedicated platform. What would settle the argument is a pilot test of both approaches, with metrics on adoption rates, data accuracy, and leadership engagement to determine which method truly drives meaningful risk discussion and action.
